items.question: What is the difference between a class instance and a struct instance after assignment?
items.answer: A class variable stores a reference to a heap object, so assignment copies the reference and both variables observe the same mutations. A struct assignment copies the fields; later mutations on one copy do not affect the other. Interviews often then ask when that copy is expensive and why Redis cache keys and coordinates are usually readonly structs.
followUps: When does boxing a struct allocate?
Why is a mutable struct in a List a trap?
items.sixtySeconds: Class: shared identity via reference. Struct: independent copy. Use class for services and identity; small immutable data as readonly struct.

items.question: Explain get, set, init, and the C# 14 field keyword.
items.answer: get reads. set mutates after construction. init allows assignment only during object initialization (constructor or object initializer). field inside an accessor is a compiler-synthesized backing field, so you can validate in set without declaring _msg yourself. Name collisions with a member named field need @field or a rename.
followUps: How does init interact with records and with-expressions?
What breaking change can field cause in existing types?
items.sixtySeconds: init is construction-time set. field is the hidden store in the accessor. Still keep fields private; properties are the API.

items.question: When do you use ref, in, and out instead of ordinary parameters?
items.answer: Ordinary parameters copy the value (or the reference for classes). ref aliases an existing variable both ways. in is a readonly alias — useful for large readonly structs so you skip the copy. out is a definite-assignment contract: the callee must write it. Do not reach for ref on every hot path; measure, and prefer readonly struct plus in.
followUps: Why can in still copy a mutable struct?
items.sixtySeconds: Ordinary first. ref = alias. in = readonly alias. out = must assign. Defensive copies bite mutable structs.

items.question: How do primary constructors and required properties change construction?
items.answer: Primary constructors (C# 12) put parameters on the type declaration and make them available in the body and field initializers. required properties (C# 11) force object initializers to set those members or the compiler errors. Together they replace telescoping constructor overloads for DTO-like types without hiding invalid empty objects.
followUps: Can a struct parameterless constructor differ from default(T)?
How do you validate primary-constructor parameters?
items.sixtySeconds: Primary ctor captures inputs on the type. required makes initializers complete. default(T) still zero-inits structs without running your ctor.

items.question: List C# access modifiers a senior should name, including file.
items.answer: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, private protected, and file for file-local types. Members default to private; top-level types default to internal. protected internal is union (assembly or derived). private protected is intersection (derived and same assembly). file is for source generators and collision-free helpers, not a member modifier on ordinary classes.
followUps: How is this different from TypeScript private?
items.sixtySeconds: CLR enforces accessibility. file-local types never leak across files. protected internal vs private protected is a favorite trap.

items.question: Should you implement a finalizer on a class that wraps SkiaSharp?
items.answer: Almost never. Implement IDisposable (and IAsyncDisposable if needed) and use using. Finalizers are a GC topic — module 14 — and they delay collection, run on a dedicated thread, and are easy to get wrong. Extension members that look like instance APIs are module 10, not a substitute for wrapping resources.
followUps: What is the Dispose pattern versus a finalizer?
Where do C# 14 extension members live in this curriculum?
items.sixtySeconds: Dispose with using. Finalizers: module 14. Extensions: module 10. Do not mix those answers.
